podcast.body: The artwork for this album features disassembled and reconstructed dolls, medical models, fetuses, and embryo-like imagery, reflecting Kurt Cobain's artistic aesthetic and fascination with human anatomy. "If you're ever look carefully at the artwork for the in-utero album, you'll see all kinds of disassembled and reconstructed dolls and medical models, fetuses and embryo like things."

podcast.body: This album was initially considered a "commercial stiff" upon its release, selling less than 200,000 copies in its first week. This performance caused some concern towards the end of Kurt Cobain's life regarding the band's commercial trajectory. "Now there was a little concern at the end of his life, because the in-utero album was almost considered to be a commercial stiff, at least initially."

podcast.body: This album, the follow-up to "Nevermind," did not achieve the major commercial success expected upon its release, selling less than 200,000 copies in its first week. A significant factor in its underperformance was the refusal of Walmart and Kmart, across all 4,000 of their stores, to stock the record due to concerns about its "offensively or go content." This commercial setback occurred amidst growing public fatigue with Kurt Cobain's persistent personal issues and his public resistance to fame. "In Udaro, the follow-up to never mind, hadn't been the major hit everyone expected."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This album, the follow-up to "Nevermind," initially fizzled upon its release in the fall of 1993, selling less than 200,000 copies in its first week. Walmart stores refused to stock it due to its artwork and some lyrical content. Fans had reportedly grown bored of Kurt's issues and his anti-star stance. "When in Yudrow came out on the fall of 1993, it really kind of fizzled."
